What the fungus is getting out of it
Mycorrhizal fungi wrap around tree roots, or push inside them, and run a fairly blunt business. They deliver water and mineral nutrients that roots struggle to reach on their own, and they charge for the service in sugar, which they cannot manufacture. The threads doing the delivery, called hyphae, are finer than cotton, and one fungus can be plugged into several trees at once, wiring them into shared plumbing whether the trees have any say in it or not.
None of that is controversial. Everything after it is.
The number that raised the stakes
In 2016 a team at the University of Basel took the question to grown timber. Using a construction crane and a web of fine tubing, Tamir Klein, Rolf Siegwolf and Christian Körner flooded the crowns of 40-metre spruce with labelled carbon dioxide, then hunted for that signature in the neighbours. They found it in beech, larch and pine. Writing in Science, they calculated that as much as 40 per cent of the carbon in a tree’s smallest roots had arrived from next door, a flow of roughly 280 kilograms per hectare per year. Körner’s verdict was blunt: a forest stops making sense as a collection of separate trees.
What happens when the donor is injured
Here is where the dying-tree story begins. In 2015 Yuan Yuan Song, Simard and colleagues stripped the needles from interior Douglas fir seedlings, some by hand and some by turning western spruce budworm loose on them, then tracked what moved into ponderosa pine seedlings potted alongside. Their paper in Scientific Reports reported that carbon made through photosynthesis shifted from the damaged firs into the pines through the fungal network, and not through soil or root contact. The pines also ramped up production of the enzymes they use to fight off pests.
Striking result, and also one experiment, in pots, on seedlings, with injury standing in for death. A tree stripped of needles is a long way from a tree dying, and a pot in a greenhouse behaves nothing like open ground.
Why a group of ecologists called it misinformation
In 2023 Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema read through the literature and came back unimpressed. Their review in Nature Ecology and Evolution tested three popular claims and judged two of them thinly supported: that these networks are widespread in forests, and that resources moving through them improve seedling performance. Field results, they argued, vary too much and carry too many alternative explanations. The third claim, that mature trees preferentially feed their own offspring and send them warnings, had no peer-reviewed published evidence at all. They also documented a habit in the field of citing the encouraging results and quietly skipping the null ones.
A separate team led by Nils Henriksson at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences pressed a different objection in New Phytologist: nobody has explained why a fungus would give sugar away. A fungus that hands a windfall to a seedling with nothing to trade back has a poor business model, and in boreal forests, the cold coniferous forests of the far north, seedlings growing close to big trees frequently do worse rather than better.
The part both camps accept
Klein and co-authors, answering the critics in Open Research Europe, hold that evidence for belowground carbon transfer is solid and accumulating, though they concede its importance to any individual tree stays unresolved. That much is common ground. What is still argued over is the route, the volume, and what any of it means for the tree on the receiving end. Labelled carbon found in a neighbour might have crossed hypha to hypha, or leaked into soil and been collected second-hand, or passed through bacteria on the way.
Which leaves the dying tree.
No published study shows an old tree sensing the end and deliberately handing its reserves to the forest around it. Settling that would mean labelling a large tree in real ground, severing the fungal links in half the plots, then waiting years for the thing to die on cue. That experiment has not been run. Until it is, the most honest account of a dying tree’s final act is that its carbon goes somewhere, and the forest is entirely unsentimental about where.
summary: Trees in forests are connected beneath the soil by mycorrhizal fungi that trade water and minerals for tree sugars, establishing shared underground plumbing. While experiments demonstrate that carbon can transfer between trees through these networks, scientists deeply debate how widespread, significant, or beneficial this resource sharing actually is. Critics argue that claims about mature trees intentionally feeding their offspring or dying trees distributing their reserves lack solid, peer-reviewed evidence in natural field settings.
key_points: Mycorrhizal fungi wrap around tree roots, delivering water and nutrients in exchange for sugars manufactured through photosynthesis.
Early and subsequent studies tracing labeled carbon have shown that carbon can move between different trees via these fungal networks.
A 2023 review by ecologists challenged popular claims about the prevalence and benefits of these networks, noting a lack of robust field evidence.
Researchers question why fungi would give away sugars to seedlings without receiving a reciprocal trade, highlighting evolutionary contradictions.
There is currently no published study proving that an old, dying tree deliberately transfers its remaining carbon reserves to the surrounding forest.

title: The Artemis II rocket and spacecraft took nearly 12 hours to crawl four miles to their launchpad at less than 1 mph—then, after carrying four astronauts around the Moon, the Orion capsule returned to Earth at nearly 25,000 mph, more than 30,000 times faster.
author: Space Daily; Mission Notes
content:
The widest speed range in the Artemis II mission began before the rocket ever left the ground. On 17 January 2026, NASA’s fully assembled Space Launch System rocket, Orion spacecraft and mobile launcher moved from the Vehicle Assembly Building to Launch Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center. The four-mile trip took nearly 12 hours.
Less than three months later, Orion brought Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen home from the Moon at close to 25,000 miles per hour. That was its speed at the beginning of atmospheric entry, not at splashdown. Even so, comparing it with the crawler’s maximum loaded speed of 0.82 miles per hour gives a ratio of more than 30,000 to one.
The arithmetic is memorable, but it is not a story about a slow old vehicle becoming a fast spacecraft. It is a story about handing four people through a chain of machines, each designed for a different part of the flight.
The first trip was a lifting problem
NASA’s record of the January rollout says the stack reached Pad 39B at 6:42 pm after a trip of nearly 12 hours. Crawler-transporter 2 had carried the roughly 11-million-pound load at no more than 0.82 miles per hour, pausing after it cleared the Vehicle Assembly Building so crews could reposition Orion’s access arm.
The crawler is hardly a small machine. It weighs about 6.6 million pounds, measures 131 feet long and 114 feet wide, and can carry as much as 18 million pounds. NASA’s Artemis II reference guide says it was designed for 2 miles per hour when unloaded and 0.83 miles per hour while carrying a rocket. Engineers choose the actual speed according to the smoothness of the ride.
That last point matters. The job was not simply to cover four miles. Hydraulic jacking, equalisation and levelling cylinders had to keep the mobile launcher level while the crawler climbed the roughly five-degree pad slope. NASA’s account of crawler operations describes the machine changing height beneath the load rather than allowing the rocket to lean with the road. Near the mounting points, positioning is measured in inches.
Nearly 12 hours included deliberate pauses
The January move was the first Artemis II rollout, made so teams could conduct pad tests and wet dress rehearsals with cryogenic propellants. It was not the final trip before liftoff. Following the tests, an upper-stage helium-flow problem sent the rocket back to the assembly building, a rollback Space Daily covered in February.
Teams repaired the problem, refreshed batteries and performed other work before SLS and Orion rolled out again on 20 March. That second trip took about 11 hours. The sequence is a useful correction to the neatest version of the story: the rocket did not crawl to the pad once and launch from there. Ground operations deliberately preserved the option to test, retreat, repair and try again.
At crawler speed, stopping costs little. With a 98-metre rocket standing vertically on top of a mobile launch tower, avoiding vibration and maintaining alignment are worth far more than arriving a few hours earlier.
Launch turned careful movement into controlled acceleration
SLS lifted off from Pad 39B at 6:35 pm EDT on 1 April with 8.8 million pounds of thrust. The rocket placed Orion into Earth orbit, where the crew checked systems and practised manual handling before the spacecraft departed for the Moon. Orion then followed a free-return trajectory, a path shaped so that lunar gravity would direct it back towards Earth.
The nearly 10-day mission covered an officially updated total of 695,081 miles. At its farthest point, the crew reached 252,756 miles from Earth. As Space Daily reported in its comparison with Apollo 13, Artemis II passed the 1970 distance record by 4,101 miles, doing deliberately what Apollo 13 had done during an emergency return.
Speed in space is also more complicated than a single peak number. SLS provided the initial acceleration, but Orion’s smaller burns controlled the route, corrected its approach and placed the crew module into the narrow entry corridor needed to reach the Pacific recovery zone.
The 25,000 mph figure belongs to entry, not splashdown
At 7:53 pm EDT on 10 April, Orion reached entry interface 400,000 feet above Earth. NASA’s live mission record described the capsule as travelling nearly 35 times the speed of sound. NASA officials rounded the figure to 25,000 miles per hour in the agency’s post-mission release.
That is when the return became an exercise in removing energy. Orion’s heat shield faced temperatures of about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit as compressed and ionised gas formed around the capsule. The crew experienced up to 3.9 times Earth’s gravity, while the plasma caused a planned communications blackout of roughly six minutes.
The atmosphere performed most of the braking before any parachute opened. At 23,400 feet, the drogue parachutes deployed and the recorded speed fell to 479 feet per second, about 327 miles per hour. At 5,400 feet the three main parachutes opened, cutting the speed below 200 feet per second before slowing Orion to roughly 20 miles per hour for splashdown at 5:07 pm Pacific time.
What the 30,000-fold contrast actually shows
The comparison uses two real speeds, but they belong to different machines and different moments. The crawler protected a tall, heavily loaded structure from unnecessary motion. SLS supplied enough thrust to leave Earth. Orion’s propulsion guided the flight. The heat shield, atmosphere and parachutes then removed nearly all the speed before the Pacific arrived.
At one end, success meant moving so slowly that engineers could monitor the load and stop. At the other, it meant entering the atmosphere at lunar-return speed and following a descent sequence that could not pause at all. Artemis II connected those regimes safely. The speed ratio is memorable because it compresses the whole mission into one number, but the real achievement was controlling every transition between them.
summary: The Artemis II mission demonstrated an immense range of speeds, starting with a 12-hour rollout where a crawler transporter moved the 11-million-pound rocket four miles to the launchpad at under 1 mph. Following a nearly 10-day lunar journey with four astronauts, the Orion capsule returned to Earth and entered the atmosphere at nearly 25,000 mph. The mission successfully managed multiple technological transitions, from careful ground transport and rocket liftoff to precise space navigation and atmospheric braking.
key_points: NASA's Artemis II rocket and Orion spacecraft were moved to Launch Pad 39B by Crawler-transporter 2, taking nearly 12 hours for a four-mile trip at a maximum speed of 0.82 mph.
The mission carried astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen on a nearly 10-day journey around the Moon.
Orion re-entered Earth's atmosphere at a speed of nearly 25,000 miles per hour, subjecting the heat shield to temperatures of about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit.
The atmosphere and a sequence of drogue and main parachutes slowed the capsule down to roughly 20 miles per hour for a Pacific Ocean splashdown.
